product.title: Bosnian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Bosnian: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Bosnian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide and noun genders, exercises, and an answer key. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up — three noun genders, the seven noun forms (padež) introduced one at a time, and the little words like sam, se, mi, ga that must sit in second place in the sentence. Includes a guide to all thirty letters, an A1 grammar summary, and a reference list of the most useful verbs with their aspect pairs.

blocks.text: Bosnian is a Slavic language — a cousin of Russian, Polish, and Czech. From a distance that sounds intimidating. Up close, it is far friendlier than its reputation, for three reasons.

**First: there are no articles.** No *the*, no *a*, no *der/die/das*. *Voz* means "train", "a train", and "the train" all at once. You will never have to decide between *a* and *the* again — the context does that job.

**Second: the spelling is completely honest.** The language reformer Vuk Karadžić left one rule that is still followed today: *Piši kao što govoriš* — write as you speak. Thirty letters, thirty sounds, one letter one sound, no exceptions. No silent letters, no historical spellings — nothing like *though, through, tough*. After the pronunciation chapter you can read any word aloud, including ones you have never seen before.

**Third: you already know some of the vocabulary.** Bosnia has absorbed words from Latin, German, Italian, and — after five centuries under the Ottoman Empire — hundreds from Turkish and Arabic. Many international words look almost the same: *muzika, problem, telefon, univerzitet, doktor, apoteka, restoran, banka, informacija, student*. Read them aloud and you understand them.

So where is the hard part? Bosnian difficulties are real, and they gather in just three places. **Nouns change their endings according to their job in the sentence** — seven forms, called *padež* (cases); English does the same job with prepositions and word order (*in, to, from, with*), Bosnian does it with endings. **Verbs change for every person** — six forms in each tense. And **little words** like *sam, se, mi, ga, ću* that stick to the second slot of the sentence and may never stand at the front.

That is why the three are not piled up at the start. Noun gender comes in unit 3, the accusative — the object form — in unit 7, the genitive in unit 8, the locative in unit 9, the dative in unit 13, the instrumental in unit 16. One case per unit, each with a clear everyday job, not as a table to memorize. The second-slot rule comes in unit 12, once there are enough little words for it to feel necessary. The past tense opens in unit 14.
The explanations are short on purpose. What is long is not the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours in fragments. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read aloud. In Bosnian that is cheap: the spelling is honest, and the Say it column marks the stressed syllable in CAPITALS.

From the very first noun, write down its **gender** with the word — not *grad*, but *grad (m)*; not *kafa*, but *kafa (f)*. Case endings, plurals, and adjectives cannot be guessed without it. This ten-second habit is what separates fluent beginners from stumbling ones.

Don't wait for perfect pronunciation before you dare to speak. Bosnians rarely meet foreigners who bother to learn their language; three words are greeted with a big smile and, almost certainly, a cup of coffee you are not allowed to refuse.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Sretno!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place, and the seven noun forms (padež) are introduced one at a time from unit 7 to unit 16.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same structure, in a deliberate order:

items: **Dialogue** — read the Bosnian aloud first, without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part most people skip, yet it is where you see how Bosnian *thinks*. Example: *Kako se zoveš?* literally means "how self you-call?", not "what's your name"; *Sviđa mi se Sarajevo* means "pleases to-me self Sarajevo".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, with pronunciation and gender.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: How to read the literal translation
items: Hyphens join pieces that are **one word** in Bosnian: *radim* → "I-work", *gradu* → "city-loc", *prijateljem* → "friend-ins".
**m, f, n** = masculine, feminine, neuter — the gender of the noun. **pl** = plural.
Case names are abbreviated in the literal line: *-acc, -gen, -dat, -loc, -ins, -voc*. Don't translate them into a natural English sentence — they only mark the form.
**self** = the little word *se*, which turns the action back on the doer: *zovem se* → "I-call self".

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to review an earlier unit — two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Bosnian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Bosnian sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Every time you meet a new noun, say three forms at once: singular, plural, and the place form. *grad → gradovi → u gradu*. *kafa → kafe → kafu*. Ten seconds per word, and cases stop being a table to memorize.
Every time you meet a new verb, say three forms: *ja*, *on*, and — from unit 14 — the past form. *radim → radi → radio sam*. Those three are enough to work out almost everything else.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Bosnian rewards that generously, because the spelling is honest — once you know the table on the next pages, you can read anything.

This chapter is short, and that is the good news. The Bosnian alphabet has **thirty letters and thirty sounds** — each letter is always read the same way, in every word, without exception. No silent letters, no combinations to memorize, no historical spellings that drift from the sound. Vuk Karadžić put the principle into words almost two hundred years ago: *Piši kao što govoriš, čitaj kako je napisano* — write as you speak, read as it is written.

Most consonants are read **much as in English** — *b, d, f, g, k, l, m, n, p, t, v* — with three small adjustments: *g* is always hard as in **go** (never as in *gem*), *s* is always as in **sun** (never *z*), and *r* is rolled or tapped, as in Spanish or Scottish English. *h* is always pronounced, a little rougher than in English. The remaining letters need one look each, and most of their sounds already exist in English.
In the **Say it** column throughout the course, syllables are separated by hyphens and the stressed syllable is written in CAPITALS: *hvala* → HVAH-lah.
Five vowels — short, pure, always the same

blocks.title: One small trap, and only one
items: **Vowels never glide.** English turns a long *o* into "oh-w" and a long *e* into "ey". Bosnian vowels stay put from start to finish: *voda* is two clean syllables, VOH-dah, not "vow-da"; *se* is "seh", not "say". In the Say it column **oh** always means this pure *o*, and **eh** always the *e* of *bed*.
Vowel length does exist in Bosnian, but at A1 it never changes the meaning — ignore it for now.

blocks.title: Four letters, two pairs — and the good news
items: ***č* vs *ć*, and *dž* vs *đ*.** The ones with ˇ (*č, dž*) are said with the tip of the tongue pulled back — a thicker, "heavier" sound, like English *church* and *John*. The ones with ´ or a stroke (*ć, đ*) are said with the tongue flat against the palate — lighter, almost "ty" and "dy". The Say it column writes both members of each pair the same way, as **ch** and **j**.

**If you mix them up, nothing collapses.** In many Bosnian towns — Sarajevo included — native speakers pronounce these pairs almost identically in everyday speech, and nobody misunderstands. What matters is knowing that they are *spelled* differently, because that affects the spelling.

**Two places worth noticing.** Almost all Bosnian surnames end in *-ić* with the soft c: *Hodžić, Begić, Kovačević*. And the future markers *ću, ćeš, će* also use the soft c; you will use them hundreds of times from unit 19 on.

blocks.text: The r that stands alone

This is the one thing in Bosnian pronunciation that has no real English counterpart, and it looks frightening on the page: words with no vowels at all. *Prst* (finger), *trg* (square), *crn* (black), *vrt* (garden), *krv* (blood), *Srbija*.

The secret: in that position, **the *r* itself becomes the core of the syllable** — rolled a little longer, with a faint *uh*-like sound appearing by itself. *Prst* sounds roughly like "purst" (with a rolled r), one syllable. Don't slip in a full *e* (not "perest"); just roll the *r* and let the sound between appear on its own. A famous phrase Bosnians use to test foreigners: *Na vrh brda vrba mrda* — "on top of the hill a willow sways", five words without a single vowel in their main syllables.
Stress

There is just one practical rule, and at A1 it is enough: **stress never falls on the last syllable** of a word with two or more syllables. So two-syllable words are always stressed at the front: *HVAH-lah, VOH-dah, ZHEH-nah, KOO-chah, DOH-broh*. Words of three or more syllables are usually stressed on the first or second syllable — and that is what the CAPITALS in the Say it column mark throughout the course.

Bosnian actually has a pitch system far more complex than that — four kinds of accent, long and short, rising and falling. Even native speakers aren't aware of it. Ignore it entirely until B1; stressing the right syllable already makes you sound clear.

blocks.title: One-letter words that lean on the next word
items: One-letter prepositions — *u* (in/to), *s* (with), *k* (toward), *v* — and the little words *je, se, mi, ti* **never stand alone when spoken**. They merge into their neighbor: *u gradu* sounds like "oo-GRAH-doo" in one breath, *kako se zoveš* sounds like "KAH-koh-seh ZOH-vehsh".

So don't try to stress these little words. Quite the opposite: say them quickly and flatly, and put your energy into the big word. This one small change does more than anything else to make your sentences sound Bosnian rather than spelled-out Bosnian.

blocks.text: Two alphabets, one language

Bosnian is officially written in **two alphabets**: Latin (*latinica*) and Cyrillic (*ćirilica*). Both are valid and convert letter for letter. In practice, the Latin alphabet is used almost everywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina — street signs, newspapers, schools, the internet — and this whole course uses Latin only. You don't need to learn Cyrillic to reach A1.

One practical note: **Croatian**, **Serbian**, and **Montenegrin** are essentially the same language, with small differences in vocabulary and spelling. What you learn in this course works directly in Zagreb, Belgrade, and Podgorica — and vice versa. The main difference: Serbian often uses the *ekavski* forms (*lepo, mleko, reka*), while Bosnian and Croatian use *ijekavski* (*lijepo, mlijeko, rijeka*). This course uses the ijekavski forms spoken in Sarajevo.

These pages are not for studying but for **coming back to**. Everything here was introduced step by step in the units, with dialogues and exercises; here it is simply collected so you can check an ending in ten seconds.
Nouns — three genders and their plurals (units 3, 5)

Exceptions worth knowing at A1: a handful of words end in a consonant but are feminine — *noć* (night), *stvar* (thing), *ljubav* (love), *riječ* (word); their plural is **-i** (*noći, stvari*). And *dijete* (child) has the plural *djeca*, which is treated as a feminine singular word.
The seven cases — singular (units 7-16)

**Two big shortcuts.** First, for masculine and neuter words **the dative and locative are identical** (*gradu, pivu*) — so the seven cases are really only six endings to remember. Second, for **inanimate masculine** nouns **the accusative is exactly the same as the nominative** (*vidim grad*), and that covers almost every object around you.
The seven cases — plural
In the plural, **the dative, locative, and instrumental always share one form** — ending in *-ima* or *-ama*. One ending for three jobs; this is one of Bosnian's biggest gifts to beginners.
Adjectives — always follow their noun (units 3, 18)

**Comparison:** *velik → veći → najveći* (big → bigger → biggest). The endings are **-ji / -iji / -ši**, and *naj-* goes on the front without exception. "Than" = *od* + genitive or *nego*: *Sarajevo je veće od Mostara* = *Sarajevo je veće nego Mostar*.
Pronouns — four sets

These short forms **may never stand at the start of a sentence** — they sit in the second slot, after the first word: *Vidim ga* (I see him/it), *Sviđa mi se* (I like it), *Kako se zoveš?* When they stack up, the order is: **li → sam/ćeš → dative → accusative → se → je**. A full example: *Jesi li mu ga dao?* (did you give it to him?).
Two verbs that hold everything up (units 1, 4)

The **short** forms are used mid-sentence and never at the front (*Ja sam Budi*, not *Sam Budi*). The **long** forms are used for short answers and for emphasis: *Jesi li student? — Jesam.* The negative is one word, with no separate *ne*: *nisam, nemam*.
Present tense — three groups (units 2, 6)

Three things worth remembering. First, **the endings *-m, -š, -Ø, -mo, -te* are the same in all three groups** — only the vowel before them (*a, i, e*) and the *oni* form differ. Second, **the *oni* form is the one you can't guess**: *-aju* in the *-am* group, *-e* in the *-im* group, *-u* in the *-em* group. Third, the dictionary form (*raditi, znati, pisati*) often doesn't tell you the group — learn verbs in their *ja* form, not the dictionary form.
Past and future (units 14, 19)

**The -o/-la/-lo form** is made from the dictionary form: drop *-ti*, add *-o* (masculine), *-la* (feminine), *-lo* (neuter), *-li/-le/-la* (plural). *Raditi → radio, radila.* *Pisati → pisao, pisala.* *Biti → bio, bila.* Only a handful need memorizing: *ići → išao, išla*; *jesti → jeo, jela*; *reći → rekao, rekla*.

**The future has two spellings, both correct:** *radit ću* (the dictionary form loses its *-i*, and *ću* stands alone) and *radiću* (joined). This course uses the first, which is usual in Bosnia and Croatia. If the verb comes after the marker, it is written in full: *Ja ću raditi.*
Aspect — two versions of each verb (unit 15)

Almost every action has **two verbs**: one for an action in progress or repeated (*nesvršeni*, imperfective), one for an action completed once (*svršeni*, perfective). *Pisati / napisati*, *čitati / pročitati*, *jesti / pojesti*, *raditi / uraditi*, *kupovati / kupiti*. In the present tense only the *nesvršeni* one is used; in the past and future, your choice decides the meaning: *pisao sam pismo* (I was writing a letter) versus *napisao sam pismo* (the letter got written).
Numbers (unit 5)

**The rule that trips everyone up:** after **1** the noun is in the normal singular (*jedan grad*); after **2, 3, 4** (and any number ending in 2-4) the noun takes the **genitive singular** (*dva grada, tri kafe, dvadeset dvije godine*); after **5 and up** it takes the **genitive plural** (*pet gradova, deset godina*). The numbers 11-14 also take the genitive plural: *dvanaest godina*.

The forty-nine verbs that hold up this whole course, with the three forms you need to work out the rest: the *ja* form, the *on* form, and the masculine past. The last column but one gives the *svršeni* (perfective) partner where there is one — that is the one you use to say the action was completed.

blocks.text: If you reach this page after really working through all twenty units — not just reading them — you can already do something real: greet people and introduce yourself, order in a café and pay, ask the way and understand the answer, make an appointment with a time and a day, tell the story of yesterday, make plans for tomorrow, and turn down an invitation politely without sounding rude. That is A1, and it is no small thing.
To move on to A2, these three things pay off fastest:

items: **Use the cases instead of memorizing the tables again.** Take the ten nouns you use most and say them every day in three sentences: *Ovo je kafa. Pijem kafu. Razgovaramo uz kafu.* The tables on the previous pages only become useful once the endings have actually come out of your mouth.

**Collect aspect pairs, not single verbs.** From now on, write every new verb down as a pair: *kupovati / kupiti*, *čitati / pročitati*. This is the biggest investment you can make before A2, because the whole past and future depend on it.

**Listen to children's news and songs.** BHRT's *Dnevnik* is too fast for now; start with songs — classic *sevdalinka* like *Kad ja pođoh na Bentbašu* have slow, repetitive lyrics, and almost every Bosnian knows them by heart. Singing forces your mouth to produce *lj*, *nj*, *č*, and the rolled *r* without thinking.

blocks.text: And one reward waiting at the end: Bosnian is **a ticket to the whole former Yugoslavia**. What you learned in this course works directly in Croatia, Serbia, and Montenegro — it is the same language, with differences about as thin as those between American and British English. Once you reach A2, four countries open up at once, and Slovenian and Macedonian stand close enough for you to guess half of them.

One last piece of advice you won't find in any grammar book: if someone in Bosnia offers you coffee, don't say no. *Kafa* there is not a drink but an invitation to sit for an hour. That is where your Bosnian will grow fastest.
*Sretno i doviđenja!*
